track.name: excel-data
track.label: Excel for Data Analysis
track.summary: From clean data to defensible answers in Excel: cleaning, Power Query, the data model and DAX, statistics, forecasting and analytical dashboards.

phases.title: Data Analysis with Pivot Tables
phases.description: Summarize and slice raw data without writing a single formula.

phases.title: Analyst Foundations: The Excel You Need First
phases.description: A compact refresher on formulas, references, Tables and modern lookups so the rest of this track can move straight into analysis.

phases.title: Cleaning & Prepping Raw Data
phases.description: Turn messy exports into analysis-ready data: text and date functions, Flash Fill, and a repeatable process for duplicates, blanks and errors.

phases.title: Modern Formulas: Dynamic Arrays, LET & LAMBDA
phases.description: Spill formulas that build a live extract or ranked list, then simplify and reuse the logic behind them.

phases.title: Power Query in Depth
phases.description: Pull data from files, folders, the web and databases, combine and reshape it, and set it up to refresh on its own — the analyst's ETL layer inside Excel.

phases.title: Data Model, Power Pivot & DAX
phases.description: Load several tables into one in-memory model, connect them properly with a star schema, and write DAX measures that respect filter context.

phases.title: Descriptive Statistics & the Analysis ToolPak
phases.description: Summarize a data set properly, test whether a relationship or a difference is real, and stop eyeballing significance.

phases.title: Forecasting in Excel
phases.description: Smooth out noise with moving averages, account for seasonality, and let Excel's own forecasting engine project a trend forward with a confidence interval.

phases.title: Optimization with Solver
phases.description: Find the best allocation of a limited resource — the mix, quantity or schedule that maximizes profit or minimizes cost within real constraints.

phases.title: Analytical Charts & Interactive Dashboards
phases.description: The chart types built for analysis rather than decoration, then a dashboard a reader can filter themselves with slicers and a timeline.

phases.title: Python in Excel
phases.description: Write real Python — pandas, plots — directly inside a worksheet cell for the analysis Excel formulas alone can't do cleanly.

phases.title: Large Data, Performance & the Path to Power BI
phases.description: Keep a growing workbook fast, and recognize the point where a report has outgrown Excel and belongs in Power BI instead.

phases.title: Capstone: End-to-End Analysis Project
phases.description: Take one messy raw dataset all the way through cleaning, Power Query, the Data Model, PivotTables, a forecast, and a one-page dashboard.

topics.title: Building Your First Pivot Table
topics.description: Turn a raw data dump into a summary in a few drags.

steps.t: Convert your source range to a Table
steps.d: Select the raw data and press Ctrl+T so the PivotTable can pick up new rows automatically.
Insert > PivotTable from the Table, and drop one field into Rows and one numeric field into Values.

steps.t: Change the summary and add a second field
steps.d: Switch Values from Count to Sum (or another summary), then add a second Rows or Columns field to break the summary down further.

topics.title: Sorting, Filtering & Excel Tables
topics.description: Structured tables that expand automatically and filter without breaking formulas.

steps.d: Right-click a value in the PivotTable and sort its row field largest-to-smallest instead of alphabetically.
Use a Row or Column field's filter dropdown to show only a subset of categories.
Add a few new rows to the underlying Table, then Refresh the PivotTable and confirm the new rows are included.

topics.title: Pivot Table Calculations & Slicers
topics.description: Custom summaries and interactive filters on top of a pivot table.

steps.d: Use Value Field Settings > Show Values As to display a value as a % of total instead of a raw sum.
Create a simple calculated field (e.g. a per-unit ratio) that isn't a column in the source data.
Insert a slicer on a category field and click through it to filter the PivotTable interactively.

topics.title: Formulas, References & Conditional Aggregation
topics.description: The formula mechanics — relative vs. absolute references — plus the conditional SUM/COUNT/AVERAGE functions an analyst writes daily.

steps.d: Write a formula that should not shift when copied, and add $ signs until it doesn't.

steps.t: Replace a nested IF with SUMIFS
steps.d: Take a total that currently depends on a helper column of TRUE/FALSE flags and rewrite it as one SUMIFS.
Extend a SUMIFS or COUNTIFS formula to filter on two conditions at once, e.g. region and date range.

topics.title: Excel Tables & Structured References
topics.description: Convert ranges into Tables so formulas, PivotTables and Power Query all keep working as rows are added.

steps.t: Convert a range to a Table
steps.d: Select your data and press Ctrl+T, then rename the Table to something meaningful.
Reference a column by name, e.g. =SUM(Sales[Amount]), instead of a cell range.
Add a new row at the bottom of the Table and confirm formulas and formatting extend automatically.

topics.title: Modern Lookups: XLOOKUP & INDEX/MATCH
topics.description: The lookup toolkit analysts actually use: XLOOKUP for new workbooks, INDEX/MATCH for anywhere XLOOKUP isn't available.

steps.d: Rewrite an existing VLOOKUP so it can look left as well as right, and add an if_not_found argument.
Use INDEX/MATCH (or XLOOKUP twice) to pull a value at the intersection of a row and column label.
Write down, for your own files, the version of Excel your collaborators use and pick XLOOKUP or INDEX/MATCH accordingly.

topics.title: Text & Date Cleanup Functions
topics.description: TRIM, CLEAN and the modern TEXTSPLIT family for stripping and slicing dirty text before it reaches a formula or a pivot.

steps.d: Wrap an imported column in TRIM(CLEAN(...)) and confirm leading spaces and non-printing characters disappear.

steps.t: Split a combined field with a formula
steps.d: Use TEXTSPLIT, TEXTBEFORE or TEXTAFTER to pull a first name, domain, or code out of a single text cell.
Convert a date that Excel is treating as text into a real date serial number and format it.

topics.title: Flash Fill & Text to Columns
topics.description: Split and reshape columns interactively, without writing a formula, when the pattern is simple and one-off.

steps.t: Trigger Flash Fill on a pattern
steps.d: Type the desired result for the first two rows of a column and press Ctrl+E to fill the rest.

steps.t: Run the Text to Columns wizard
steps.d: Split a delimited or fixed-width column into separate fields using Data > Text to Columns.
Note which of your cleanup steps need to survive a data refresh (formula/Power Query) versus a single cleanup (Flash Fill).

topics.title: Duplicates, Blanks & Errors
topics.description: A repeatable pass to catch the three things that quietly break downstream totals: duplicate rows, blank cells, and formula errors.

steps.d: Highlight duplicate values with conditional formatting, review them, then run Remove Duplicates.

steps.t: Find every blank in a range
steps.d: Use Go To Special > Blanks to select all empty cells in a column and fill or flag them in one pass.
Add IFERROR or IFNA around a lookup so a missing match shows a clear message instead of #N/A.
Write a short checklist (dupes checked, blanks checked, errors checked) you re-run on every new data pull.

topics.title: FILTER, SORT, UNIQUE & SEQUENCE for Analysis
topics.description: Four functions that spill a live, formula-driven extract onto the sheet — the core toolkit for ad hoc analysis without a helper table.

steps.d: Use FILTER to pull only the rows matching a condition (e.g. one region, one status) into a spill range.
Wrap the FILTER result in SORT so the extract comes out ordered by a metric, largest first.
Use UNIQUE to build a distinct list of categories, then feed it into a data-validation dropdown.
Use SEQUENCE to create a running list of periods or IDs without typing or dragging.

topics.title: LET — Naming Steps Inside a Formula
topics.description: Break a long nested formula into named, reusable pieces so it calculates once and reads like a sentence.

steps.d: Take a formula that calculates the same lookup or ratio more than once and count the repeats.
Rewrite the formula with LET, giving each intermediate result a plain-English name.
Confirm a colleague could read your LET formula and explain what each named step does.

topics.title: LAMBDA — Writing Custom, Reusable Functions
topics.description: Package a LET formula into your own named function, callable anywhere in the workbook like a built-in.

steps.d: Turn a working LET formula into a LAMBDA with named parameters, and test it in one cell first.
Save the LAMBDA under a short name (e.g. RATIO) via Name Manager so it's callable like a native function.
Build a LAMBDA that calls itself to solve something a loop would normally handle, such as summing digits or walking a list.

topics.title: Connecting to Data: Files, Folders, Web & Databases
topics.description: Power Query's four-phase model — Connect, Transform, Combine, Load — and the connectors an analyst reaches for most: folders, the web, and databases.

steps.d: Load a CSV or Excel file through Data > Get Data and watch Power Query record each transform as an Applied Step.
Point Power Query at a folder of same-format files and use Combine & Load to stack them into one table.

steps.t: Pull a table from a web page
steps.d: Import a table from a public web page and note which parts of the page Power Query can and can't parse.

topics.title: Combining Queries: Merge, Append & Unpivot
topics.description: The three moves that turn several ragged tables into one clean one: join sideways, stack vertically, and flatten wide layouts into long ones.

steps.t: Merge two queries on a key
steps.d: Join a lookup table onto a fact table using Merge Queries, and choose whether to keep unmatched rows.
Stack several same-structure queries into one with Append Queries, and confirm columns line up by name, not position.
Take a cross-tab layout (one column per month) and use Unpivot Columns to turn it into Attribute/Value rows a PivotTable can consume.

topics.title: Shaping Data: Custom Columns & the M Language
topics.description: Go beyond the point-and-click transforms by writing custom columns and reading the M code behind every step.

steps.d: Use Add Column > Custom Column to derive a field (e.g. margin, flag, bucket) with an M expression.
Open a query's Advanced Editor and identify the let/in structure and the name of each step.

steps.t: Edit one step's M by hand
steps.d: Change a single line of M code directly (e.g. a filter condition or column name) instead of redoing it through the UI.

topics.title: Parameters & Refresh: Making Queries Reusable
topics.description: Parameterize a query so the same logic runs against a new file, date range or environment, then keep it current with refresh.

steps.t: Convert a hard-coded value to a parameter
steps.d: Right-click a fixed date, path or number in a query step and convert it to a parameter.

steps.t: Reuse the parameter in another query
steps.d: Reference the same parameter from a second query so both stay in sync when it changes.
Refresh a query manually, then check the option to refresh it automatically when the workbook opens.

topics.title: Data Model, Relationships & Star Schema
topics.description: Load multiple tables into Excel's Data Model and connect them with real relationships instead of VLOOKUPs, using a star schema so it stays fast and simple.

steps.t: Load two tables into the Data Model
steps.d: Add a fact table and a lookup table to the Data Model via Power Pivot or 'Add to Data Model'.
Drag the matching key columns together in Diagram View to define a one-to-many relationship.

steps.t: Redraw your model as a star
steps.d: Sketch which of your tables is the fact table and which are dimension tables, and check every dimension connects directly to the fact table.

topics.title: DAX Fundamentals: CALCULATE & Filter Context
topics.description: The one idea that unlocks DAX: every measure runs inside a filter context, and CALCULATE is how you change it.

steps.d: Create a New Measure that sums or averages a column, and drop it into a PivotTable to see it recalculate per cell.
Use CALCULATE with a filter argument to compute a value that ignores one of the PivotTable's own filters (e.g. a grand-total-style ratio).

steps.t: Explain filter context in your own words
steps.d: Write one sentence describing why the same measure returns a different number in every cell of a PivotTable.

topics.title: DAX Time Intelligence & Power Pivot Measures
topics.description: Purpose-built DAX functions for year-to-date, prior-period and year-over-year measures, on top of a proper date table.

steps.d: Add a contiguous date table to the Data Model and mark it as the model's date table.
Use TOTALYTD to compute a running year-to-date total that responds to slicers.
Use SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR (or DATEADD) to add a year-over-year comparison measure next to the current one.

topics.title: Calculated Fields, Calculated Items & GETPIVOTDATA
topics.description: Add a calculation directly inside a PivotTable, and pull a stable value out of one with a formula that survives layout changes.

steps.d: Use Fields, Items, & Sets > Calculated Field to add a metric the source data doesn't already have, such as a margin percentage.

steps.t: Pull a value out with GETPIVOTDATA
steps.d: Reference one PivotTable cell by clicking it from a formula outside the table and see Excel auto-generate GETPIVOTDATA.

steps.t: Decide when to turn auto-GETPIVOTDATA off
steps.d: Explain the tradeoff: GETPIVOTDATA survives a pivot's layout changing, but breaks quick fill-across formulas.

topics.title: Grouping, Advanced Layouts & PivotTables from the Data Model
topics.description: Group raw dates and numbers into readable buckets, and build a PivotTable straight from the Data Model instead of a single table.

steps.t: Group dates into months and quarters
steps.d: Right-click a date field in a PivotTable and group it by Months, Quarters and Years.

steps.t: Group a numeric field into bins
steps.d: Group a numeric row field (e.g. order size) into fixed-width bins by setting a start, end and interval.

steps.t: Build a PivotTable from the Data Model
steps.d: Insert a PivotTable from 'Tables in Workbook Data Model' instead of a single range, and check fields from both tables appear together.

topics.title: Descriptive Statistics & the Analysis ToolPak
topics.description: Enable Excel's built-in statistics add-in and use it to generate a full summary — mean, median, std dev, kurtosis — in one pass instead of one formula at a time.

steps.d: Turn on the add-in via File > Options > Add-ins so Data Analysis appears on the Data tab.
Point the Descriptive Statistics tool at one numeric column and generate the full summary table.
Look up what skewness or kurtosis in the output actually means for your data and write one sentence about it.

topics.title: Correlation & Regression
topics.description: Quantify whether two variables move together, then fit a line through them and read what the ToolPak's regression output is actually telling you.

steps.d: Use the Analysis ToolPak's Correlation tool (or CORREL) across several numeric columns and scan for the strongest relationships.
Use Data Analysis > Regression with one Y range and one or more X ranges, ticking Residual Plots.
Identify R² in the regression statistics block, the F-significance in the ANOVA block, and the p-value on each coefficient.

topics.title: Hypothesis Testing in Excel
topics.description: Decide whether a difference between two groups is likely real, using a t-test and a properly interpreted p-value.

steps.d: Decide between a paired, equal-variance, or unequal-variance two-sample t-test based on how your two groups relate.
Use Data Analysis to run the t-test and produce the output table with the p-value in it.

steps.t: State the conclusion in plain English
steps.d: Write one sentence translating the p-value into a decision, without saying 'proves' or 'significant' incorrectly.

topics.title: Moving Averages & Seasonality
topics.description: Smooth a noisy series with a moving average, then separate the seasonal pattern from the underlying trend.

steps.d: Write an AVERAGE formula over a fixed window (e.g. 3 or 12 periods) and copy it down a time series.
Divide each period's actual value by its centered moving average to get a seasonal index per period.
Divide the raw values by their seasonal index to see the underlying trend without the seasonal swing.

topics.title: FORECAST.ETS & the Forecast Sheet
topics.description: Let Excel's exponential-smoothing engine project a time series forward automatically, with a confidence interval attached.

steps.d: Select a two-column time series and use Data > Forecast Sheet to generate a projection and chart in one step.
Open Options in the Forecast Sheet dialog and compare the result with seasonality set automatically versus manually.
Use FORECAST.ETS directly in a cell to compute one forecasted point, matching what the Forecast Sheet drew.

topics.title: Setting Up Solver: Objective, Variables & Constraints
topics.description: Translate a real optimization question — what mix maximizes profit? — into an objective cell, variable cells and constraints Solver can work with.

steps.d: Turn on Solver via File > Options > Add-ins so it appears in the Analysis group on the Data tab.
Build a worksheet with an objective cell (e.g. total profit) that depends on a small number of variable cells.
Add at least two constraints (e.g. a capacity limit and a non-negativity rule) and run Solver to find the optimal variable values.

topics.title: Solver Methods & Sensitivity Reports
topics.description: Pick the right solving method for the shape of your problem, then read the sensitivity report to see how robust the optimal answer really is.

steps.d: Decide between Simplex LP, GRG Nonlinear and Evolutionary based on whether your formulas are linear, smooth nonlinear, or contain integer/IF logic.
After solving, request the Sensitivity report and locate the shadow price on a binding constraint.
State in plain English what the shadow price tells you about buying one more unit of a constrained resource.

topics.title: Analytical Chart Types: Histogram, Box Plot, Pareto, Scatter & Waterfall
topics.description: Five chart types built to answer a specific analytical question — distribution, spread, the vital few causes, relationship, and the walk from one total to another.

steps.d: Insert a Histogram chart on a numeric column and adjust the bin width until the shape is readable.
Build a Box and Whisker chart with one box per category to compare medians and outliers at a glance.
Build a Pareto chart on a set of causes/categories and read off which ones account for roughly 80% of the total.

steps.t: Show the walk from start to end
steps.d: Build a Waterfall chart that walks from an opening value through several positive/negative changes to a closing value.

topics.title: Interactive Dashboards: Slicers, Timelines & Layout
topics.description: Turn a set of PivotTables and charts into a single-page dashboard a reader can filter themselves, without touching a formula.

steps.d: Insert a slicer on a PivotTable field and connect it to more than one PivotTable or chart at once.
Insert a Timeline on a date field so the reader can drag to change the date range instead of picking from a list.
Arrange your charts and slicers onto a single printable dashboard sheet, and remove anything that isn't answering a question.

topics.title: Getting Started with Python in Excel
topics.description: Write your first =PY formula and see Python run in the cloud against your worksheet data, no separate install required.

steps.d: Select a cell, use Insert Python (or type =PY), and write a one-line Python expression against a range of cells.
Pass an Excel range or Table into a Python cell and confirm it arrives as a pandas DataFrame.

steps.t: Return a result to the grid
steps.d: Convert a Python output back to Excel values (not just a Python object) so other formulas can use it.

topics.title: Python for Analysis: pandas & Visualization
topics.description: Use the pandas, Matplotlib and Seaborn libraries that ship with Python in Excel to do analysis a formula alone would struggle with.

steps.d: Use a pandas method (e.g. groupby or drop_duplicates) inside a Python cell to do a cleanup step formulas make awkward.
Generate a Seaborn or Matplotlib chart from a Python cell and place it on the worksheet as a static image.
Write one sentence on when you'd reach for Python in Excel instead of a native formula or Power Query step, for your own work.

topics.title: Large Data & Performance
topics.description: Diagnose why a big workbook has gone slow, and the specific habits — volatile functions, full-column references, unfolded queries — that usually cause it.

steps.d: Set Calculation Options to Manual on a large workbook and recalculate with F9 while you make several changes.
Search your workbook for NOW, TODAY, RAND, OFFSET or INDIRECT and replace one with a non-volatile equivalent.
Open a Power Query step and check the folding indicator to see whether the transform is running at the source or after it loads.

topics.title: Excel to Power BI: Making the Jump
topics.description: Recognize the signals that a report has outgrown Excel, and see how far a Power Pivot Data Model already carries over to Power BI.

steps.d: Check your workbook against the classic signals: rebuilt on a schedule, shared with many people, or nearing performance limits.

steps.t: Map your Data Model to Power BI
steps.d: Note which parts of your existing Data Model, relationships and DAX measures would carry over directly to Power BI.
Work through a free 'Get started with Power BI' module to see the same star-schema and DAX ideas in the Power BI Desktop interface.

topics.title: Capstone: End-to-End Analysis Project
topics.description: Every skill in this track, applied in sequence to one dataset: clean it, load it, model it, analyze it, forecast it, and present it on one page.

steps.d: Choose a free multi-table dataset (e.g. a Kaggle sales or retail dataset) with the kind of duplicates, blanks and inconsistent formats real data has.

steps.t: Clean and load it with Power Query
steps.d: Import it through Power Query, fix text/date issues, remove duplicates, and load it into the Data Model.

steps.t: Model it and write two DAX measures
steps.d: Build relationships in a star schema and write at least one CALCULATE-based measure and one time-intelligence measure.
Build a PivotTable-driven analysis, add a simple forecast, and lay it all out on one slicer-driven dashboard sheet with a short written summary of what you found.
